meta.title: Strategy, the balanced scorecard and strategic profitability analysis
meta.summary: Differentiation and cost leadership, the four perspectives of the balanced scorecard, building a scorecard and strategy map, splitting operating income into growth, price-recovery and productivity, engineered and discretionary costs, and scorecard pitfalls.

videos.title: Choosing a strategy
videos.take: Companies compete by differentiation or cost leadership; accounting should measure progress on the chosen strategy

scenes.say: Before you can measure performance, you need to know what you're trying to achieve. That's strategy.

scenes.heading: Two broad strategies
scenes.say: A company can compete through product differentiation, offering something customers value and will pay a premium for, or through cost leadership, delivering acceptable products at the lowest cost.

scenes.heading: Forces that shape strategy
scenes.say: Michael Porter's five forces shape which strategy can work: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, and the bargaining power of customers and suppliers. Cheap imported e-bikes and powerful battery suppliers both pressure Tallgrass.
Tallgrass chooses differentiation: rugged bikes built in Minnesota, backed by local dealer service and a long warranty, priced above imports.
The accounting system should then measure progress on that strategy. A differentiator should track quality, customer loyalty and price premiums, not just cost per bike.

scenes.q: A company sells basic e-bikes at the lowest price in the market through high-volume production. Its strategy is:
scenes.say: Quick check. A company sells basic e-bikes at the lowest price through high volume. What's its strategy? Pause and pick.

videos.title: The balanced scorecard
videos.take: The balanced scorecard links financial, customer, internal process and learning-and-growth measures to strategy

scenes.say: Financial results tell you what happened, too late to change it. The balanced scorecard adds measures that lead to future results.
The balanced scorecard, developed by Robert Kaplan and David Norton in the 1990s, translates strategy into a set of performance measures across four perspectives.

scenes.heading: Four perspectives
items: Financial: did the strategy create value?
Customer: are target customers satisfied and loyal?
Internal business process: what must we excel at?
Learning and growth: people, systems, culture
scenes.say: Financial: did the strategy create value for shareholders? Customer: are we winning in our target market? Internal business process: what operations must we excel at? Learning and growth: do we have the people, systems and culture to improve?

scenes.heading: Cause and effect, bottom up
scenes.say: The perspectives link by cause and effect. Better-trained assemblers lead to fewer defects and faster delivery, which lead to loyal customers, which lead to higher margins. Drawn out, this is a strategy map.
The balance is between financial and nonfinancial measures, internal and external, and leading indicators that predict results versus lagging indicators that report them.

scenes.q: Hours of training per assembler belongs to which perspective?
scenes.say: Quick check. Hours of training per assembler belongs to which perspective? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Tallgrass's scorecard
videos.take: Each measure needs a target and must connect to the strategy

scenes.say: Here's the scorecard Ana built to track Tallgrass's differentiation strategy.

scenes.heading: Tallgrass scorecard, 2027
scenes.say: Financial: grow operating income by ten percent. Customer: hold a five percent share of the regional market. Internal process: fewer than three warranty claims per hundred bikes. Learning and growth: ninety percent of assemblers certified on the new motor system.

scenes.heading: 2027 results
scenes.say: Results: operating income grew eight percent, below target. Market share slipped to four point four percent. But warranty claims fell to two point six, and ninety-two percent of assemblers are certified.

Read the scorecard as a story. Quality improved, yet share fell. Either the effect hasn't reached customers yet, or quality isn't what's driving their choice. Remember the Cargo bike problem from Lecture 5: range and price may matter more.

sub: change the strategy or the measures
scenes.say: That's the value of the scorecard: it tests the strategy's cause-and-effect assumptions. If the links don't hold, managers should rethink the strategy or the measures.

scenes.q: Which is a leading indicator for Tallgrass's financial results?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which is a leading indicator of financial results? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B. Dealer satisfaction should predict future sales and margins.

videos.title: Growth, price recovery and productivity
videos.take: Splitting the change in operating income shows whether it came from growth, pricing power or efficiency

scenes.say: Operating income rose. But why? Strategic analysis splits the change into growth, price recovery and productivity.

scenes.heading: Tallgrass, before fixed costs
scenes.say: In 2026, Tallgrass sold a thousand bikes at $2,300, with material kits at $1,000 and seven assembly hours a bike at twenty-eight dollars. In 2027, eleven hundred bikes at $2,400, kits at $1,040, and assembly took only six hours a bike, at thirty dollars an hour.

scenes.heading: Change in operating income: $194,000
scenes.say: The growth component, a hundred more bikes at 2026 prices and productivity, added $110,400. The price-recovery component, the price rising faster than input prices, added $50,600. The productivity component, eleven hundred fewer assembly hours than 2026 efficiency would need, at thirty dollars, added $33,000.
For a differentiator, price recovery is the key test: Tallgrass raised prices by more than its input costs rose, a sign customers value the brand.

sub: Fewer inputs per unit of output
scenes.say: A cost leader would look for most of its gains in productivity: producing the same output with fewer inputs.

scenes.q: Which component shows whether Tallgrass can pass higher costs on to customers?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which component shows whether Tallgrass can pass higher costs on to customers? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Engineered and discretionary costs
videos.take: Engineered costs have a clear input–output link; discretionary costs don't, so they're managed by judgment

scenes.say: Some costs can be precisely linked to output. Others depend on management judgment. They're managed differently.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of cost
scenes.say: Engineered costs have a clear cause-and-effect link to output: materials, assembly labor, machine time. Discretionary costs, like advertising, research and training, have no measurable link; managers decide how much to spend.

scenes.heading: Engineered capacity: assembly
scenes.say: Take assembly. Twelve workers supply twenty-one thousand six hundred hours a year. Three thousand bikes at six hours need eighteen thousand. Thirty-six hundred hours, two workers' worth, are unused.
Unused engineered capacity can be filled by growing sales, redeployed to other work, or reduced. Downsizing should be done carefully, keeping the skills a differentiator needs.

sub: this year's profit, harms the future
scenes.say: Discretionary costs are the easiest to cut when profits are tight, because the harm is delayed. Cutting R&D or training to hit this year's target can damage a differentiator's future. The scorecard's learning and growth measures help guard against that.
Quick check. Which is a discretionary cost? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C. There's no precise link between training spending and output.

videos.title: Making scorecards work
videos.take: Keep scorecards short, linked to strategy and to rewards; add sustainability where it matters

scenes.say: Many scorecards fail. Here's how to make one work.

scenes.heading: Common pitfalls
items: Too many measures: focus is lost
Measures not linked by cause and effect
No targets, or no link to rewards
Ignoring the scorecard when finances are bad
scenes.say: Common pitfalls: too many measures, so nobody can focus; measures with no cause-and-effect link to strategy; no targets or no link to rewards; and dropping the nonfinancial measures as soon as profits fall.
A rule of thumb: no more than fifteen to twenty-five measures, three to six per perspective, each tied to the strategy map.

scenes.heading: Adding sustainability
scenes.say: Many companies now add environmental, social and governance measures. For Tallgrass: battery recycling rate, workplace injuries, and suppliers' compliance with its code of conduct, important given risks in battery supply chains.
And review the scorecard regularly. When strategy changes, the measures must change too.

scenes.q: A scorecard has 60 measures. What's the main risk?
scenes.say: Quick check. A scorecard has sixty measures. What's the main risk? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B: with so many measures, managers can't focus on what drives the strategy.

warmup: What does your favorite brand compete on: price or something else? How would you measure whether its strategy is working?
Introduces differentiation vs cost leadership and the need for nonfinancial measures.
acts: Classify the strategy of: a discount online e-bike seller; a Minnesota maker of hand-built titanium bikes; a big-box retailer's store-brand bike.
Write one measure for each perspective for Redwood Valley Creamery, which competes on artisanal quality.
Financial: price premium vs commodity cheese; customer: repeat buyers; process: % blocks graded premium; learning: cheesemaker training hours.
Draw a strategy map for Tallgrass's goal of raising Cargo bike share.
Learning: battery engineering skills → process: longer-range design, faster dealer delivery → customer: Cargo share, satisfaction → financial: revenue growth, margin.
2028: 1,200 bikes at $2,450; kits $1,060; 6,900 hours at $31. Using 2027 as base (6 hours per bike), compute the three components (ignore fixed costs).
Assembly has 24,000 hours of capacity at $30; 3,300 bikes need 6 hours each. Cost of unused capacity?
Cut Tallgrass's scorecard of 40 measures to 12. Which would you keep?

3 per perspective tied to the strategy map: OI growth, price premium, cash flow; share, dealer satisfaction, repeat riders; warranty claims, delivery time, new-model time; certification, engineer retention, IT uptime.
case: The CEO wants to cut training

Tallgrass's 2027 operating income growth was 8% against a 10% target. To hit 2028's target, the CEO proposes cutting the $120,000 dealer and assembler training budget and delaying the battery R&D project ($200,000). Ana's scorecard shows warranty claims falling as certification rose, and the strategic analysis shows most 2027 income growth came from price recovery.
Classify the proposed cuts as engineered or discretionary.
What would the cuts do to 2028 income and to the scorecard?
How do the strategic analysis results argue against the cuts?

Both are discretionary. They add $320,000 to 2028 income but hurt learning-and-growth and, later, quality, price premium and share. Price recovery shows customers pay for quality, so cutting what sustains it undermines the strategy. Recommend keeping them, finding productivity gains or unused-capacity reductions instead, and resetting targets if needed.
exam: Explain the four perspectives of the balanced scorecard, giving one measure for each for an e-bike maker following a differentiation strategy.

Financial (OI growth, price premium); customer (market share, satisfaction); internal process (warranty claims, delivery time, new-product development time); learning and growth (training, certification, retention). Linked by cause and effect.
Explain the growth, price-recovery and productivity components of the change in operating income, and which matters most for a cost leader and for a differentiator.

Growth: change in output at prior-year prices and productivity. Price recovery: change in output prices relative to input prices. Productivity: fewer inputs for the output. Cost leader: productivity; differentiator: price recovery.

Financial results report what has already happened.

Assembly hours actually used 6,600; hours that 2026 productivity would need 7,700; 2027 rate $30. Productivity component?
